Voiced alveolar nasal [n], close back rounded vowel [u], and alveolar tap or trill [r]; the accented core of the name.
Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus open vowel [a]; the final syllable closes the theonym.

pronunciation.approximation: 'nee-NOOR-tah' — stress the second syllable; the final a is open and level, not drawn out.

pronunciation.note: Ninurta is Tier 2: the Unicode restoration N-I-N-U-R-T-A preserves only the capitalized ASCII form and carries no distinctive diacritic or non-ASCII letter that the ASCII form loses. It is a straightforward philological capitalization, not a phonological reconstruction hub. Standard Assyriology writes Ninurta; the PuniCodex form simply gives the name its proper noun shape.

domains.title: Lord of the Earth
domains.subtitle: War · Agriculture · Storms
domains.lead:
Ninurta is the Mesopotamian deity in whom the weapons of war and the tools of the field are not opposites but a single office. His name is usually interpreted as 'lord of the earth' (Sumerian nin 'lord/lady' + urta/urša 'earth'), and his cult spans the storm-mace, the plough, and the stone quarry. In the Sumerian poems Lugal-e and Angimdimma, and in the Akkadian Anzû Epic, he is the champion the great gods summon when order has been stolen or the mountain rebels.

Unlike the remote sovereignty of Anû or the atmospheric kingship of Enlīl, Ninurta acts. He hunts the rebel Anzû through the mountains, recovers the Tablet of Destinies, and afterward assigns every defeated stone its place in the human economy. His mythology is therefore a charter myth for metallurgy, agriculture, and kingship alike: the god who breaks the enemy also names the useful rock.

mythology.lead: Ninurta's myths are myths of restorative force: a threat appears, the younger warrior-god is dispatched, and the aftermath is not merely victory but the reorganization of the world. He is the patron of the campaign that ends in a treaty with matter itself.

myths.title: The Theft of the Tablet of Destinies
myths.text: In the Akkadian Anzû Epic, the storm-bird Anzû steals the ṭuppi šīmāti, the Tablet of Destinies, from Enlīl while the high god bathes. Without it, the gods lose their power to decree fates. Anu first asks Adad, then Girra, then Shara to recover it; each refuses when he sees Anzû wearing the tablet. Ninurta alone accepts. He rides to battle on his storm-chariot, hurls winds and arrows, and finally sends his enchanted mace Sharur to strike Anzû's heart. The tablet is restored to Enlīl, and Ninurta's supremacy among the warrior gods is proclaimed. The story is preserved in the Standard Babylonian version from Nineveh (Tablet I–III) and older Akkadian fragments.

myths.title: Ninurta and the Hostile Stones
myths.text: The Sumerian poem Lugal-e ('O king, storm of all the lands') recounts Ninurta's campaign against the demon Asag and his stone army in the mountain land of the Kur. Asag has seized the territory and paralyzed cultivation. Ninurta defeats him, shatters the rebel stones, and then — in a long catalog — names each stone and assigns it a purpose: lapis lazuli for the temple, flint for the sickle, limestone for the mason, carnelian for the seal-cutter. The poem is thus a mythic encyclopedia of Mesopotamian mineralogy and a charter for the extraction of raw materials.

myths.title: The Return to Nippur
myths.text: In Angimdimma ('Ninurta's return to Nippur'), the victorious god returns to the Ekur, Enlīl's temple, and is praised by the assembled deities. The poem rehearses his titles — warrior of Enlīl, master of the mace, ploughman of the gods — and asserts that his victories are not personal glory but the enforcement of cosmic order. The text underlines the theological pattern of Mesopotamian kingship: the young hero acts, then presents his triumph to the father-god.

myths.title: Ninurta and Ningirsu
myths.text: In the city-state of Lagaš, the local warrior-god Ningirsu ('lord of Girsu') was venerated as the divine patron of the ruling dynasty and the protector of the irrigation system. Gudea, the ensi of Lagaš, rebuilt Ningirsu's temple and recorded the god's commands in his famous cylinder inscriptions. Over time Ningirsu was identified with Ninurta, so that by the first millennium BCE the two names often refer to a single deity. The Girsu tradition emphasizes Ninurta's agricultural and hydraulic role: the warrior who secures the floodplain and makes the fields bear.

syncretism:
Ninurta's profile overlaps with several Mesopotamian and neighboring deities, sometimes as identity, sometimes as delegated function.

In the south, Ningirsu of Girsu was gradually merged with Ninurta, while retaining a distinct local cult well into the second millennium BCE. In the north, the Assyrian national god Aššur absorbed many of Ninurta's martial traits, so that temple hymns from Assur praise Aššur as the slayer of Anzû. Marduk of Babylon later inherited Ninurta's storm-combat role in the Enuma Elish, where Marduk defeats Tiamat with winds and bonds — a victory that parallels Ninurta's over Asag. The Hittite storm-god Teššub and the Canaanite Baꜥal share the same Indo-Mediterranean storm-warrior type. There is no direct Greek equivalent, though Árēs overlaps in war and Hēphaistos in craft; Ninurta's combination of battlefield and forge is distinctively Mesopotamian.
culturalLegacy:
Ninurta's legacy survives in the idea of the ordered earth as the fruit of conflict.

The long catalog of stones in Lugal-e is one of the earliest surviving examples of a learned encyclopedic text in cuneiform — a precursor to later Mesopotamian lexical lists and perhaps to the genre of technical handbook. His association with the plough and irrigation underlies the Mesopotamian doctrine that kingship secures fertility: the king wages war so that the peasant may plough. In modern fantasy and games, Ninurta appears as a storm-warrior or earth-shaker, often conflated with generic 'Thunderbird Slayer' archetypes. PuniCodex preserves the name in its simple ASCII form as a Tier-2 display, honoring the fact that for this theonym the canonical tradition has passed down a plain Latin transliteration without a recoverable distinctive mark. The name still means: the lord who turns battle into harvest.
extendedMeditation:
Ninurta is the god of the aftermath. He does not only kill the demon; he inventories the stones. He does not only recover the Tablet of Destinies; he restores the power of the gods to decree fate. His mythology is a charter for every civilization that must transform raw violence into durable order — the army that becomes a police force, the mine that becomes a temple, the flood that becomes irrigation.

To name Ninurta is to remember that agriculture itself was once a conquest: the forest cleared, the stone broken, the river channelled. The plough is a weapon that has learned peace. The mace is a tool that remembers war. In Ninurta the two are held together without contradiction, because for the Mesopotamians the earth's abundance was not a given but the result of divine labor imposed upon chaos.

archaeology: Archaeological evidence for Ninurta centers on temples at Nippur (the Ekur complex, where he is Enlīl's warrior son), Girsu/Telloh (the sanctuary of Ningirsu, patron of the Lagaš state), and Kalhu/Nimrud, where Ashurnasirpal II dedicated a major Ninurta temple whose reliefs show the god as an archer. Foundation figurines, votive mace-heads, and royal inscriptions of kings from Gudea to the Assyrian emperors invoke Ninurta as the source of martial success and agricultural prosperity.
